In addition to the direct benefits of automation, it may bring other advantages. For example, schemes for 20 __________ will be more workable, especially in towns and cities, resulting in fewer cars on the road.

According to the University of Michigan Transportation Research Institute, there could be a 43 percent drop in 21 __________ of cars. However, this would mean that the yearly 22 __________ of each car would, on average, be twice as high as it currently is. This would lead to a higher turnover of vehicles, and therefore no reduction in automotive manufacturing.

questionSections.heading: Questions 38–40
instructions: Complete the summary below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes 38–40 on your answer sheet.
questionSections.summary: The writer has experience of a large number of 38 __________, and was the first stranger that certain previously 39 __________ people had encountered. He believes there is no need for further exploration of Earth’s 40 __________, except to answer specific questions such as how buffalo eat.

questions.prompt: the leaves of the tree are 1 __________ in shape
questions.evidence: The tree is thickly branched with dense foliage of tough, dark green oval leaves
questions.distractors: ‘dark green’ describes colour and ‘tough’ describes texture; only ‘oval’ names the shape.

questions.prompt: the 2 __________ surrounds the fruit and breaks open when the fruit is ripe
questions.evidence: The fruit is encased in a fleshy husk. When the fruit is ripe, this husk splits into two halves
synonymSubstitutions: breaks open ↔ splits into two halves
questions.distractors: ‘aril’ surrounds the seed, not the fruit; ‘ridge’ is the line along which the husk splits.

questions.prompt: the 3 __________ is used to produce the spice nutmeg
questions.evidence: the two spices nutmeg and mace, the former being produced from the dried seed
synonymSubstitutions: is used to produce ↔ being produced from
questions.distractors: The aril produces mace, while the husk is not identified as the source of either spice.

questions.prompt: the covering known as the aril is used to produce 4 __________
questions.evidence: the two spices nutmeg and mace, the former being produced from the dried seed and the latter from the aril
synonymSubstitutions: from the aril ↔ the aril is used to produce
questions.distractors: ‘nutmeg’ is the former spice and comes from the seed; the latter spice is mace.

questions.prompt: In the Middle Ages, most Europeans knew where nutmeg was grown.
questions.evidence: the Arabs were the exclusive importers of the spice to Europe ... they never revealed the exact location of the source
synonymSubstitutions: knew where nutmeg was grown ↔ knew the exact location of the source
most Europeans ↔ contradicted by exclusive importers keeping the location secret
questions.distractors: Nutmeg was widely valued in Europe, but popularity does not mean Europeans knew its source; the passage explicitly says the location was concealed.

questions.prompt: The VOC was the world’s first major trading company.
questions.evidence: By 1617, the VOC was the richest commercial operation in the world.
questions.distractors: ‘Richest’ describes its status in 1617; the text never says it was the first major trading company.

questions.prompt: Following the Treaty of Breda, the Dutch had control of all the islands where nutmeg grew.
questions.evidence: the Dutch and British arrived at ... the Treaty of Breda ... The British agreed ... The Dutch now had a monopoly over the nutmeg trade
synonymSubstitutions: control of all the islands ↔ monopoly over the nutmeg trade
questions.distractors: Before the treaty, Run remained British; the statement asks about the situation following the treaty, when the Dutch monopoly was complete.

questions.prompt: Nutmeg was brought to Europe by the 8 __________.
questions.evidence: the Arabs were the exclusive importers of the spice to Europe
synonymSubstitutions: was brought to Europe by ↔ were the importers ... to Europe
questions.distractors: Venetian merchants bought nutmeg in Europe; the Portuguese reached the source later. The importing group named for this period is the Arabs.

questions.prompt: the disease known as the 9 __________
questions.evidence: people across Europe were dying of the plague ... they decided nutmeg held the cure
questions.distractors: ‘disease’ is the category word already supplied; ‘plague’ is the one-word name required.

questions.prompt: put 10 __________ on nutmeg to avoid it being cultivated outside the islands
questions.evidence: all exported nutmeg was covered with lime to make sure there was no chance a fertile seed ... would leave the islands
synonymSubstitutions: avoid cultivation outside ↔ no chance a fertile seed ... would leave
questions.distractors: Plantation zones describe where production was concentrated; the substance physically applied to nutmeg was lime.

questions.prompt: obtained the island of 11 __________ from the British
questions.evidence: if the British would give them the island of Run ... The British agreed
synonymSubstitutions: obtained from ↔ the British would give them
questions.distractors: Manhattan was what the Dutch gave Britain in return; Run was the island the Dutch obtained.

questions.prompt: 1770 – nutmeg plants were secretly taken to 12 __________
questions.evidence: in 1770 ... successfully smuggled nutmeg plants to safety in Mauritius
questions.distractors: Grenada received some plants later; the dated 1770 destination was Mauritius.

questions.prompt: 1778 – half the Banda Islands’ nutmeg plantations were destroyed by a 13 __________
questions.evidence: in 1778, a volcanic eruption ... caused a tsunami that wiped out half the nutmeg groves
questions.distractors: The eruption caused the destructive event, but the grammar ‘by a’ and the passage’s direct agent point to ‘tsunami’.

questions.prompt: reference to the amount of time when a car is not in use
questions.evidence: At present, the average car spends more than 90 percent of its life parked.
synonymSubstitutions: amount of time ↔ 90 percent of its life
questions.distractors: D discusses trip numbers and mileage, not the proportion of a car’s life spent unused.

questions.prompt: mention of several advantages of driverless vehicles for individual road-users
questions.evidence: it may be possible to be productive, to socialise or simply to relax ... older or disabled travellers ... may be able to enjoy significantly greater travel autonomy
questions.distractors: C gives system-wide sharing benefits; B lists several direct benefits to people travelling.

questions.prompt: reference to the opportunity of choosing the most appropriate vehicle for each trip
questions.evidence: drivers will have the freedom to select one that best suits their needs for a particular journey
synonymSubstitutions: opportunity of choosing ↔ freedom to select
questions.distractors: D considers how many vehicles are needed; only E discusses selecting a vehicle for a journey.

questions.prompt: an estimate of how long it will take to overcome a number of problems
questions.evidence: many challenges ... can most probably be conquered within the next 10 years
synonymSubstitutions: how long ↔ within the next 10 years
questions.distractors: F names the challenges but gives no time estimate; G supplies both the problems and the ten-year estimate.

questions.prompt: a suggestion that the use of driverless cars may have no effect on the number of vehicles manufactured
questions.evidence: This faster rate of turnover may mean that vehicle production will not necessarily decrease.
synonymSubstitutions: no effect on the number manufactured ↔ production will not necessarily decrease
questions.distractors: C predicts fewer vehicles may meet demand, but D qualifies this by explaining why production may not fall.

questions.prompt: most motor accidents are partly due to 19 __________
questions.evidence: more than 90 percent of road collisions involve human error as a contributory factor
synonymSubstitutions: partly due to ↔ involve ... as a contributory factor
questions.distractors: ‘safety’ is the motive for research; ‘human error’ is the stated contributing cause and fits the two-word limit.

questions.prompt: schemes for 20 __________ will be more workable
questions.evidence: initiatives for car-sharing become much more viable
questions.distractors: ‘automated vehicles’ names the technology, while the schemes explicitly named are for car-sharing.

questions.prompt: a 43 percent drop in 21 __________ of cars
questions.evidence: automated vehicles might reduce vehicle ownership by 43 percent
questions.distractors: The same study says mileage would double, not drop; ‘ownership’ is the quantity reduced by 43 percent.

questions.prompt: the yearly 22 __________ of each car would, on average, be twice as high
questions.evidence: vehicles’ average annual mileage would double as a result
questions.distractors: ‘turnover’ becomes faster later, but the measured yearly quantity that doubles is mileage.

questions.prompt: Which TWO benefits of automated vehicles does the writer mention?
options: A Car travellers could enjoy considerable cost savings.
B It would be easier to find parking spaces in urban areas.
C Travellers could spend journeys doing something other than driving.
D People who find driving physically difficult could travel independently.
E A reduction in the number of cars would mean a reduction in pollution.
questions.evidence: it may be possible to be productive, to socialise or simply to relax ... older or disabled travellers – may be able to enjoy significantly greater travel autonomy
synonymSubstitutions: doing something other than driving ↔ productive/socialise/relax
questions.distractors: A invents personal cost savings; B confuses less parking demand with easier space-finding; E invents a pollution claim. Only C and D are stated.

questions.prompt: Which TWO benefits of automated vehicles does the writer mention?
options: A Car travellers could enjoy considerable cost savings.
B It would be easier to find parking spaces in urban areas.
C Travellers could spend journeys doing something other than driving.
D People who find driving physically difficult could travel independently.
E A reduction in the number of cars would mean a reduction in pollution.
questions.evidence: C is supported by productive/social/leisure use of driving time; D is supported by greater autonomy for older or disabled travellers.
synonymSubstitutions: physically difficult ↔ challenged by existing mobility models
questions.distractors: This shares the same A–E set and either-order answer pair as Question 23; A, B and E are not stated benefits.

questions.prompt: Which TWO challenges to automated vehicle development does the writer mention?
options: A making sure the general public has confidence in automated vehicles
B managing the pace of transition from conventional to automated vehicles
C deciding how to compensate professional drivers who become redundant
D setting up the infrastructure to make roads suitable for automated vehicles
E getting automated vehicles to adapt to various different driving conditions
questions.evidence: communities [must] trust and accept automated vehicles ... the vehicle works reliably in the infinite range of traffic, weather and road situations
synonymSubstitutions: general public has confidence ↔ communities trust and accept
different driving conditions ↔ infinite range of traffic, weather and road situations
questions.distractors: B, C and D are not discussed: the passage mentions regulation/liability, but not transition pace, compensation or road rebuilding.

questions.prompt: Which TWO challenges to automated vehicle development does the writer mention?
options: A making sure the general public has confidence in automated vehicles
B managing the pace of transition from conventional to automated vehicles
C deciding how to compensate professional drivers who become redundant
D setting up the infrastructure to make roads suitable for automated vehicles
E getting automated vehicles to adapt to various different driving conditions
questions.evidence: The two stated hurdles are reliable operation across varied situations and societal trust and acceptance.
synonymSubstitutions: adapt ↔ works reliably ... it might encounter
questions.distractors: The same either-order pair applies to Questions 25 and 26. Options B–D add challenges not stated in section F.

questions.prompt: The writer refers to visitors to New York to illustrate the point that
options: A exploration is an intrinsic element of being human.
B most people are enthusiastic about exploring.
C exploration can lead to surprising results.
D most people find exploration daunting.
questions.evidence: This questing nature of ours undoubtedly helped our species ... and a visitor negotiate the subways of New York.
synonymSubstitutions: intrinsic element of being human ↔ questing nature of ours / helped our species
questions.distractors: B claims enthusiasm, C claims surprising results and D claims fear; none is stated. New York is an everyday example of the universal questing instinct.

questions.prompt: According to the second paragraph, what is the writer’s view of explorers?
options: A Their discoveries have brought both benefits and disadvantages.
B Their main value is in teaching others.
C They act on an urge that is common to everyone.
D They tend to be more attracted to certain professions than to others.
questions.evidence: we all have this enquiring instinct, even today
synonymSubstitutions: common to everyone ↔ we all have
questions.distractors: A and B are not discussed; D reverses the point—the instinct appears in all sorts of professions, not only certain ones.

questions.prompt: The writer refers to a description of Egdon Heath to suggest that
options: A Hardy was writing about his own experience of exploration.
B Hardy was mistaken about the nature of exploration.
C Hardy’s aim was to investigate people’s emotional states.
D Hardy’s aim was to show the attraction of isolation.
questions.evidence: used the landscape to suggest the desires and fears of his characters. He is delving into matters ... common to humanity.
questions.distractors: A confuses character exploration with Hardy’s own travel; B contradicts the writer’s approval; D narrows ‘uncultivated land’ into an attraction to isolation.

questions.prompt: In the fourth paragraph, the writer refers to ‘a golden age’ to suggest that
options: A the amount of useful information produced by exploration has decreased.
B fewer people are interested in exploring than in the 19th century.
C recent developments have made exploration less exciting.
D we are wrong to think that exploration is no longer necessary.
questions.evidence: as if the process of discovery is now on the decline, though the truth is that we have named only one and a half million ... and there may be more than 10 million
synonymSubstitutions: no longer necessary ↔ process of discovery ... on the decline
wrong to think ↔ though the truth is
questions.distractors: A, B and C are not claimed. The unexplored species, oceans and brain show exploration remains necessary.

questions.prompt: In the sixth paragraph, when discussing the definition of exploration, the writer argues that
options: A people tend to relate exploration to their own professional interests.
B certain people are likely to misunderstand the nature of exploration.
C the generally accepted definition has changed over time.
D historians and scientists have more valid definitions than the general public.
questions.evidence: Each definition ... tends to reflect the field of endeavour of each pioneer ... the prominent historian ... the cutting-edge scientist
questions.distractors: The writer does not rank definitions, accuse anyone of misunderstanding, or trace a historical change in a single accepted definition.

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph, the writer explains that he is interested in
options: A how someone’s personality is reflected in their choice of places to visit.
B the human ability to cast new light on places that may be familiar.
C how travel writing has evolved to meet changing demands.
D the feelings that writers develop about the places that they explore.
questions.evidence: how a fresh interpretation, even of a well-travelled route, can give its readers new insights
synonymSubstitutions: cast new light ↔ fresh interpretation / new insights
places that may be familiar ↔ well-travelled route
questions.distractors: A and D shift attention to personality or feelings; C invents an industry history. The sentence focuses on reinterpretation of familiar routes.

questions.prompt: He referred to the relevance of the form of transport used.
questions.evidence: Wilfred Thesiger ... ‘If I’d gone across by camel when I could have gone by car, it would have been a stunt.’
synonymSubstitutions: relevance ↔ would have been a stunt
questions.distractors: The other explorers discuss novelty, usefulness, physical contact, social change or returning home; only Thesiger contrasts transport modes.

questions.prompt: He described feelings on coming back home after a long journey.
questions.evidence: Peter Fleming talks of the moment when the explorer returns to the existence he has left behind with his loved ones ... encounters his other self
synonymSubstitutions: coming back home ↔ returns to the existence ... with his loved ones
questions.distractors: Thesiger discusses travel method, not homecoming; the quoted home-return experience is explicitly attributed to Fleming.

questions.prompt: He worked for the benefit of specific groups of people.
questions.evidence: Robin Hanbury-Tenison, a campaigner on behalf of remote so-called ‘tribal’ peoples
synonymSubstitutions: worked for the benefit of ↔ a campaigner on behalf of
questions.distractors: The professions of the other four are named, but only Hanbury-Tenison is described as campaigning on behalf of a group.

questions.prompt: He did not consider learning about oneself an essential part of exploration.
questions.evidence: To him, exploration meant bringing back information from a remote place regardless of any great self-discovery.
questions.distractors: Fleming describes a changed sense of self, but the statement asks who explicitly treats self-discovery as non-essential: Thesiger.

questions.prompt: He defined exploration as being both unique and of value to others.
questions.evidence: Ran Fiennes ... ‘An explorer is someone who has done something that no human has done before – and also done something scientifically useful.’
synonymSubstitutions: unique ↔ no human has done before
of value to others ↔ scientifically useful
questions.distractors: Bonington stresses physical novelty but not usefulness; Fiennes explicitly combines unprecedented action with scientific value.

questions.prompt: The writer has experience of a large number of 38 __________
questions.evidence: I’ve done a great many expeditions and each one was unique.
synonymSubstitutions: a large number of ↔ a great many
questions.distractors: ‘voyages’ appears later as an age that has passed; the writer’s own experience is explicitly a great many expeditions.

questions.prompt: certain previously 39 __________ people
questions.evidence: I’ve lived for months alone with isolated groups of people all around the world, even two ‘uncontacted tribes’.
synonymSubstitutions: previously encountered no stranger ↔ uncontacted / isolated
questions.distractors: ‘remote’ occurs elsewhere, but the official key accepts the exact source descriptors ‘uncontacted’ or ‘isolated’.

questions.prompt: no need for further exploration of Earth’s 40 __________, except to answer specific questions such as how buffalo eat
questions.evidence: We know how the land surface of our planet lies; exploration of it is now down to the details – the habits of microbes, say, or the grazing behaviour of buffalo.
synonymSubstitutions: how buffalo eat ↔ grazing behaviour of buffalo
questions.distractors: The deep sea and underground are explicit exceptions; the already known domain is the (land) surface, matching the official variants.
